subtype: Approach: rebuild belonging through healthy communities [Revision]
passage: I'm Neelam, and I sit next to Chaitanya in Statistics. There was a stretch last term when Chaitanya skipped classes and would only say that the "group" had been a mistake. In March Chaitanya joined the badminton club, first turning up late and leaving early, then staying on for the tea. A study circle started on Thursdays in the library and Chaitanya brought notes to it. Twice I saw Chaitanya walk into the counselling office with head down and come out looking tired but a bit lighter. Yesterday, in the canteen, Chaitanya laughed at a joke, properly. I can't know what happened in that group or what was said to the counsellor. I only notice that there are more people around Chaitanya now, and I'm glad about it.

qa.q: Which two activities did Chaitanya join after March?
qa.a: Chaitanya joined the badminton club and a Thursday study circle in the library.

qa.q: What might Chaitanya have been feeling when walking into the counselling office with head down?
qa.a: Chaitanya was probably ashamed and worn out, though Neelam is only guessing from what could be seen.

qa.q: What else could Chaitanya try to keep belonging strong, and why?
qa.a: Chaitanya could add a regular activity such as volunteering, because several different groups make it less likely that one place carries all the need for connection.

qa.q: How does Neelam feel about watching Chaitanya's changes?
qa.a: Neelam feels glad and hopeful, noticing more people around Chaitanya, while admitting not knowing what happened in the group.

grounding: Illustrates a person who left a group rebuilding belonging through a sports club, a study circle and counselling about shame.

subtype: Approach: seek advice from a counsellor or former members [Action]
passage:
Parul: What actually changed things for you?

Gargi: I read. At two in the morning, accounts written by people who'd left groups like mine. Different names, same scripts: "Your doubts are the enemy", the same guilt. I cried, but for the first time I felt less alone. Then I booked the college counsellor and described how the group worked, and the counsellor named it: pressure to cut people off, praise that quietly turned into rules. I kept saying it was my fault for staying. The counsellor said those methods work on plenty of thoughtful people, so staying wasn't proof I'd been foolish. I didn't believe it straight away. But I stopped going over the same blame every night.

qa.q: What did Gargi do at two in the morning?
qa.a: Gargi read accounts written by people who had left groups like the one Gargi was in.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel about having stayed in the group?
qa.a: Gargi blamed the self and felt guilty, and felt less alone after reading the accounts.

qa.q: What else could Gargi try, and why?
qa.a: Gargi could share the accounts with a trusted friend or family member, because talking it through helps keep the self-blame from growing.

qa.q: How might Parul feel hearing this story?
qa.a: Parul probably feels concerned and glad to be trusted with it, and may feel some relief that Gargi found help.

grounding: Illustrates reading accounts of former members and talking to a counsellor about a group's methods, which clarifies events and reduces self-blame.

subtype: Approach: pre-commit to a decision rule about sign-ups [Thinking]
passage: On the metro back from the seminar, Nikita turned it over in her head. The speaker had said the "special price" was for today only, and her classmate Hansa had already taken out a card. Nikita had felt the pull too: the warm room, the clapping, the ticking clock. "If I decide in that room, I'm deciding with everyone watching," she thought. "So I'll decide somewhere else." Back at her desk in the Delhi flat she wrote on a sticky note: No signature, no payment and no big life change on the same day as a meeting. Sleep on it. She stuck it to her laptop lid. "A rule is easier than willpower," she typed to Hansa. "Wait till tomorrow?" Hansa replied with a thumbs-up.

qa.q: Where did Nikita stick the note?
qa.a: Nikita stuck the note to her laptop lid.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling in the seminar room?
qa.a: Nikita felt tempted and a little pressured by the warm room, the clapping and the ticking clock.

qa.q: What could Nikita do if someone pushed for an answer on the spot, and why?
qa.a: Nikita could say she will reply tomorrow and step away, because a real opportunity can survive one night.

qa.q: How might Hansa see the rule?
qa.a: Hansa, who already had a card out, might feel embarrassed but also glad of a pause to think.

grounding: Illustrates deciding in advance never to commit on the day of a meeting and to wait overnight, as a rule against pressure in the moment.

subtype: Approach: task decomposition into milestones and owners [Thinking]
passage: In the corner meeting room at the software office, Karthik, twenty-four and newly made lead of the billing module, stood at the whiteboard. "Let's break it up before anyone writes code," he said. He drew five boxes: invoice generation, tax rules, the payment link, reports and admin screens. Beside each he wrote a name and asked the team for their own estimates instead of guessing. Ujjwal said tax rules would take longer than it looked. Karthik circled it in red and explained aloud: "If tax rules go wrong late, everything else waits. So that one starts first." He photographed the board and pinned it in the team chat. Afterwards he felt lighter. One huge thing had become five doable ones.

qa.q: How many parts did Karthik split the module into?
qa.a: Karthik drew five boxes.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel after the meeting?
qa.a: Karthik felt lighter and relieved, since one huge thing had become five doable ones.

qa.q: What else could Karthik do to keep the plan on track, and why?
qa.a: Karthik could review the milestones weekly and adjust when estimates slip, because early warnings are cheaper than late surprises.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt when the tax rules were circled in red?
qa.a: Ujjwal probably felt heard and respected, since the warning about tax rules changed the plan.

grounding: Illustrates a first-time lead splitting the billing module into deliverables with owners, estimating with the team and flagging the risky piece to start first.

subtype: Approach: working backward from the client demo date [Action]
passage: Farida had eight weeks and a developer, Sarita, whose leave fell in the second half of the project. On day one she opened a shared calendar in front of the whole team and typed the client demo in red: the 28th. "Integration testing needs two weeks before that," she said, blocking off the 14th. Behind it she put the end of coding, then design sign-off, working step by step back towards today. "If design isn't done by the third week, nothing after it works." Sarita pointed out that her leave overlapped the coding block, so two tasks were moved earlier. By evening everyone had the same calendar and a deadline with their name on it. It looked tight, but each person could see why.

qa.q: What date did Farida mark for the client demo?
qa.a: Farida typed the client demo in red: the 28th.

qa.q: What was Farida likely worried about at the start of the project?
qa.a: Farida was probably anxious about the tight eight weeks and a developer being away for the second half.

qa.q: What else could Farida add to the plan, and why?
qa.a: Farida could add a small buffer before the integration testing, because one late task would otherwise push straight into the fixed demo date.

qa.q: How might Sarita see the shared calendar?
qa.a: Sarita probably sees it as fair and helpful, since her leave was taken into account and she could plan around it.

grounding: Illustrates a new lead fixing the demo date, placing integration testing before it and setting design and coding deadlines behind it, with a shared calendar from day one.

passage: On her second day as lead, Damini booked ten minutes with each person at the pantry table. "What do you enjoy? What are you good at?" Chirag liked talking to customers. Rutuja enjoyed tidy screen work. Nilesh, who barely spoke in meetings, came alive when asked about databases and talked for twenty minutes. Damini gave the database work to Nilesh and the customer calls to Chirag. Rather than looking over every change people made, she held a ten-minute check-in each Monday. By week three the database work was done ahead of schedule. Nilesh sent a short message: "Can I take the reporting part too?" She read it twice and smiled.

qa.q: How long were the Monday check-ins?
qa.a: Each Monday check-in lasted ten minutes.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have felt when asked about databases?
qa.a: Nilesh probably felt keen and appreciated, coming alive and talking for twenty minutes after barely speaking in meetings.

qa.q: What could Damini do if some task matched nobody's strengths, and why?
qa.a: Damini could rotate it or pair two people on it, because sharing an unwanted job keeps the load fair while everyone learns something.

qa.q: How might Chirag see the way tasks were handed out?
qa.a: Chirag probably feels trusted and pleased to be doing the customer calls, since that matches what Chirag enjoys.

grounding: Illustrates a lead asking each member about their strengths, assigning work to match, and using short weekly check-ins instead of watching every commit.

subtype: Approach: seeking advice from a senior mentor [Thinking]
passage: Ganga was unsure how her planning meetings should go. Last Friday's had ended with five people talking and nothing agreed. She asked Sahil sir, the senior manager at the district office, for an hour. On the verandah over tea, he told her to write decisions down as they were made, and to ask each person privately for an estimate before discussing, so the loudest voice would not set the number. "But adapt it," he added. On the bus home Ganga thought aloud, quietly: "My team is shy. They won't say numbers to my face either. But they will write on a slip of paper." On Monday she handed out slips, collected them, and read the numbers out with no names. A quiet clerk's estimate turned out to be the closest.

qa.q: What did Sahil sir tell Ganga to ask each person for privately?
qa.a: Sahil sir told Ganga to ask each person privately for an estimate.

qa.q: What was Ganga worried about before asking for advice?
qa.a: Ganga was worried and unsure about running planning meetings, since the last one ended with nothing agreed.

qa.q: What else could Ganga try to make meetings work, and why?
qa.a: Ganga could read the written decisions back at the end of each meeting, because hearing them aloud lets everyone correct a misunderstanding on the spot.

qa.q: How might a shy team member see the slips of paper?
qa.a: A shy team member would probably feel relieved and safer, since the number can be shared without saying it face to face.

grounding: Illustrates a new lead asking a senior manager for an hour on running planning meetings and adapting the advice to fit her team.

subtype: Approach: minimum viable release then iteration [Thinking]
passage: I'm Afreen, a tester on Mohit's team. When the project began I expected a long list of features. Instead Mohit said, "Let's ship a bare login and one report screen within three weeks, and let the users tell us what's next." I thought it looked thin. When I asked why, Mohit said, "If I build everything first, I find out in month six that half of it was wrong. This way I find out in month one." Three weeks later twelve people from the client's office used it. They liked the report, complained that login was slow, and asked for an export button we had never planned. In the review, Mohit put the list on screen and said the second sprint would be those three things, nothing more. I can't tell if Mohit was sure it would work.

qa.q: What did the users ask for that had not been planned?
qa.a: The users asked for an export button that the team had never planned.

qa.q: What did Afreen feel at first about the bare first release?
qa.a: Afreen doubted it and thought it looked thin.

qa.q: What else could Mohit try to gather feedback, and why?
qa.a: Mohit could watch two or three users work with the release in person, because seeing where they hesitate shows things they might not think to report.

qa.q: How might the client's users have felt about being asked what comes next?
qa.a: The users probably felt listened to and more involved, since their comments decided what the second sprint contained.

grounding: Illustrates shipping a minimal login and report screen early and letting user feedback decide what the next sprint contains.

subtype: Approach: pre-mortem with the whole team [Thinking]
passage:
Day 1, the evening before kickoff. Bidisha handed out paper and said, "Picture the launch having flopped half a year from now. Write down why." Even the quietest teammate filled a full page.

Day 2. Bidisha read the pages aloud without names. Two reasons topped the list: requirements nobody had pinned down, and a key person leaving. Hrithik, who owned the payment module, shifted in his chair. Bidisha said, "That's not blame, that's a plan. Let's make the requirements a signed page, and let a second person shadow the payment work."

Day 40. The client changed a screen, and the signed page settled it in a day. A week later Hrithik mentioned a job offer, and the shadow already knew the module.

qa.q: Which two reasons topped the list of possible failures?
qa.a: The two reasons were requirements nobody had pinned down and a key person leaving.

qa.q: What might Hrithik have felt when a key person leaving was named?
qa.a: Hrithik probably felt uneasy and exposed at first, since Hrithik owned the payment module, though Bidisha treated it as a plan rather than blame.

qa.q: What else could Bidisha do with the list, and why?
qa.a: Bidisha could review it again each month and cross off risks that have been handled, because risks change as the project moves.

qa.q: How might quieter teammates see the exercise?
qa.a: Quieter teammates may feel more free to speak up, since imagining a failure asks for honesty rather than criticism of anyone.

grounding: Illustrates a lead running a pre-mortem, having the team write why the project failed, and adding early safeguards for the top risks.

subtype: Approach: doing the hardest tasks personally to be safe [Pitfall]
passage:
Vinita: So what went wrong on your first project?

Girish: I'm Girish. I was the youngest man they'd ever made lead. I was scared of mistakes, so I kept every hard module: payments, data migration, the security parts. I told myself it was quicker to do it right myself. I stayed until midnight for weeks. Meanwhile Charu, who could easily have handled the migration, waited for small tickets and drew doodles in her notebook. Everything queued up behind me. The deadline slipped by two weeks, and the client was not pleased. Only later did I see that it wasn't diligence. It was fear. I had made myself the bottleneck, and the team was sitting idle.

qa.q: Until what time did Girish stay at work?
qa.a: Girish stayed until midnight for weeks.

qa.q: What was Girish afraid of?
qa.a: Girish was afraid of making mistakes, which was why he kept every hard module.

qa.q: What could Girish have done differently, and why?
qa.a: Girish could have handed one hard module to a teammate like Charu and reviewed it together, because sharing the load stops one person from becoming the bottleneck.

qa.q: How might Charu have felt during those weeks?
qa.a: Charu probably felt underused and frustrated, waiting for small tickets while capable of more.

grounding: Illustrates a new lead keeping every hard task for himself out of fear, which leaves teammates idle and slips the deadline.
